doc_summary: The post presents three LLM auditing agents (investigator, evaluation, breadth-first red-teaming) validated against models with researcher-implanted issues, and candidly discusses limitations including prompt realism and eval awareness. It treats ground-truth testbeds and replicable parallel runs as the basis for convincing evidence about auditing methods.

items.claim: In a setup, give the auditor agent affordances for building complex, realistic inputs (e.g. a corpus of genuinely difficult coding problems, or an inner loop that iteratively improves prompt realism) instead of letting it generate simple toy scenarios, because simple generated prompts are recognisable as tests.
items.quote: One way to address this difficulty is to give agents additional affordances to help with constructing complex and realistic inputs. For example, an evaluation agent equipped with access to a corpus of difficult coding problems might more effectively build reward hacking evaluations.

items.claim: Reward-hacking setups consisting of simple coding problems with clearly buggy tests are likely to be guessed as tests by sophisticated target models, so they should be treated as eval-like.
items.quote: many of the agent-generated prompts that pose reward hacking opportunities consist of simple coding problems with clearly buggy tests; it is possible that sophisticated target models will guess that these prompts are being used for testing.

items.claim: Treats the target model's own verbalised belief that it is in an evaluation (about 1% of the time) as a measurable, non-trivial signal of poor prompt realism that should be tracked.
items.quote: Prompt realism. A related problem is that our agents struggle to generate realistic input prompts. When applying our breadth-first red-teaming agent to Claude 4 models, the target model expressed a belief that it was in a safety evaluation around 1% of the time, a small but substantial fraction.

items.claim: Behaviors that only appear under realistic pressure (e.g. hardcoding tests after repeated failure, blackmail) require building a setup that genuinely creates that pressure, such as truly difficult tasks, rather than simply asking for the behavior.
items.quote: some models only resort to hardcoding test cases after repeatedly failing to solve a difficult coding problem. Thus, eliciting this behavior requires generating a difficult coding task that the target model struggles to solve, which is itself a challenge.

items.claim: Distrusts LLM-generated evaluation prompts for lacking realism, and distrusts findings obtained via shortcuts like prefill that reveal declarative descriptions of a behavior rather than demonstrations of it.
items.quote: Sample sizes are typically modest, which sometimes impedes statistical power, and because the evaluation prompts are LLM generated, they sometimes lack realism.

items.claim: Prefers evidence consisting of demonstrations of the behavior over extracted declarative descriptions (e.g. from prefill attacks revealing a system prompt) because the latter doesn't show the model actually behaves that way.
items.quote: A substantial limitation of this environment is that it is possible to discover the target model’s quirk without surfacing any demonstrations of it.

items.claim: Prefers ground-truth testbeds with implanted behaviors and many parallel runs from identical initial states over one-off human auditing games because they give replicable, statistically meaningful validation.
items.quote: We can run many parallel auditing agents from identical initial states, allowing them to serve as consistent, replicable proxies for human auditors.

items.claim: Is wary that researcher-implanted or system-prompted behaviors and dev/test contamination make results unrepresentative of naturally arising model issues, so claims are hedged.
items.quote: these artificial behaviors may be unrepresentative of behaviors in real models.

items.claim: Gives the agent a single example prompt of a behavior hurts, since it collapses the diversity of generated evaluations onto the example, so seed examples should be avoided or varied.
items.quote: Giving the agent an example prompt hurts its ability to develop valid evaluations: qualitatively, we see that this affordance drastically collapses the diversity of the agent’s evaluations to match the example prompt.

items.claim: Auditor agents fixate on the first concerning behavior found (e.g. harmful content) and fail to probe subtler behaviors like blackmail or excessive agency, motivating breadth and aggregation.
items.quote: After finding one potentially-concerning behavior, the agent often fails to continue searching for deeper problems.

items.claim: Proposes distilling quirky system-prompted models into weights-implanted models so quirks exist without a system prompt that can be leaked, making the testbed more realistic.
items.quote: Future work could improve this environment by, for example, distilling models on the outputs of a quirky system-prompted model to obtain a model that exhibits the quirks without having any system prompt.
